content.title: About
content.content: Hazelnuts are the edible seeds of the hazel tree (Corylus avellana), native to temperate regions of Europe and Asia. The nuts have a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. Hazelnuts are eaten raw, roasted, and are used in baking, desserts, spreads, and chocolate confections.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hazelnut belongs to the birch family and is most closely related to the walnut.
There are two main types: sweet (edible) and bitter, the latter contains cyanogenic glycosides and is not meant to be eaten raw.
Ancient Greeks and Romans already used hazelnuts in cuisine and medicine.
Hazelnuts are processed into paste (hazelnut spread), oil, flour, and flavorings for confectionery.
Hazelnut blossoms appear early in spring before the leaves unfold.

items.title: Rich in vitamin E
items.content: Hazelnuts are a good source of vitamin E, a powerful antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Provides healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: The majority of fats in hazelnuts are monounsaturated, supporting heart health.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium in hazelnuts supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Provides protein and fiber
items.content: Hazelnuts supply plant protein and dietary fiber, helping to promote satiety.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Compared with many other nuts, hazelnuts contain a notable amount of calcium.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to hazelnuts, ranging up to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Hazelnuts are calorie-dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Whole hazelnuts can pose a choking risk for young children.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Hazelnuts contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hazelnuts can be enjoyed as a snack, added to granola, yogurt, salads, baked goods, or processed into paste and oil. Soaking or roasting softens them and makes skin removal easier. Opt for unsalted or lightly salted varieties.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store hazelnuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent oil rancidity. Discard nuts that smell bitter, sharp, or stale.
